requirements: Start crawling from given seed URLs
Extract text data from crawled web pages for language model training
Recrawl to keep data fresh including newly added or updated pages
Store crawled data up to 5 years
Scale to crawl approximately 1 billion pages per month (~400 pages/sec average) or handle 10 billion pages in advanced design
Enforce politeness to avoid overloading any single host (limit concurrent requests, add delays)
Fault tolerance to recover and resume after failures
Avoid infinite loops and excessive re-crawling of same content or URLs
Ability to prioritize URLs by importance (PageRank, traffic, update frequency, etc.)
Extensible to support new content types with minimal redesign
Maintain URL and content seen structures to avoid duplicate crawling and storage
Efficient storage for large volumes (petabytes scale) with hybrid memory/disk approach
Pipeline design to separate fetching, parsing, extracting, and storage stages for scalability and failure isolation
assumptions: Average webpage size ~500KB (S1) or ~2MB in planning worst-case (S2)
Seed URLs provided or can be derived by domain/topic/country partitioning
Crawler will focus on HTML text only, ignoring other media types initially
Freshness achieved by prioritizing important pages and recrawling based on update history
Web is modeled as a directed graph; crawling is BFS traversal across URLs
Crawler runs distributed worker threads, each handling one host queue to enforce politeness
Failures occur mainly at fetch stage; retries use exponential backoff with max attempts before marking site offline
URLs and content deduplication done using hash structures (e.g. Bloom filters)
Large-scale crawler requires storage in PB range for 5 years storing billions of pages
Use of cloud storage (S3 or equivalent) for storing fetched HTML and extracted text blobs
Backend queues (Kafka, SQS, Redis, or similar) effectively handle URLs to crawl and retries with mechanisms for delay and dead-letter queues
Text extraction and URL extraction stages combined but can be separated if needed
Crawl-delay from robots.txt is obeyed by crawler worker threads

alternatives.name: Depth-First Search (DFS) vs Breadth-First Search (BFS)
advantages: BFS provides better coverage of diverse hosts and freshness of newly discovered URLs
BFS maintains layers of URLs for prioritization and politeness enforcement
disadvantages: DFS risks deep traversal into a single site leading to politeness violations and resource wastage

alternatives.name: Single Monolithic Crawler vs Multi-Stage Pipeline Architecture
advantages: Multi-stage pipeline isolates failures, allowing retrying only failed stages
Easier to scale each stage independently (fetching, parsing, storage)
Facilitates changes in text extraction without re-fetching HTML
disadvantages: More complex system with greater operational overhead
Requires state management between stages to track progress and ensure idempotence

alternatives.name: In-memory URL frontier vs Hybrid disk/memory URL frontier
advantages: In-memory offers faster enqueue/dequeue operations and low latency
Hybrid approach enables handling URL frontier scale of hundreds of millions without memory limits
disadvantages: In-memory approach not durable, risks data loss on crash
Disk approach slower but durable, requires careful buffering to avoid bottlenecks

alternatives.name: Use of Kafka vs AWS SQS for URL queue
advantages: Kafka keeps immutable logs with consumer offset for precise progress tracking and fault tolerance
SQS provides message visibility timeout and redrive policy supporting exponential backoff and dead letter queues out of the box
disadvantages: Kafka requires custom implementation for retries/backoff logic
SQS may have higher latency and depends on cloud provider

failure_modes: Crawler stalls on unresponsive or slow hosts
Infinite loops due to repeated URLs without effective URL seen checks
Overloading web servers if politeness delays are not enforced
Disk bottlenecks in URL frontier if buffering is insufficient or scanning too frequent
Loss of crawl progress on node failure if queue/storage state is not correctly maintained
Duplicate content storage increases storage cost without content seen checks
Incorrect priority assignment causing important pages to be crawled late or infrequently
Changes in page format breaking text extraction process without decoupling extraction stage
Crawler ignoring robots.txt policies causing legal/compliance issues

evidence.claim: Estimated 1 billion pages per month equals ~400 QPS, requiring ~500 TB per month storage and ~30 PB for 5 years
Web crawler components include URL frontier, HTML downloader, DNS resolver, content parser, content seen filter, URL extractor, URL filter, URL seen filter, and URL storage
URL frontier must enforce politeness by mapping hosts to separate FIFO queues and worker threads, downloading one page at a time per host with delay
Prioritization of URLs in frontier improves crawling of important/recent/updated pages
Content duplication is detected by hashing web page content to prevent storing duplicate data
BFS traversal is preferred over DFS to avoid deep traversal of single hosts and improves breadth coverage
Robustness requires handling malformed pages, unresponsive servers, malicious links and system crashes
Multi-stage pipeline separates URL fetching and text+URL extraction stages to improve fault tolerance and scalability
Queues such as Kafka or SQS hold URLs, message visibility timeout supports retry with exponential backoff; dead-letter queues handle unrecoverable failures
Text extraction stage can be updated independently without re-fetching HTML
Crawler should obey robots.txt rules and crawl-delay directives to enforce politeness and compliance
Storage of raw HTML and extracted text use cloud blob storage like S3 for scalability and durability

uncertainties: Exact method for seed URL selection and coverage trade-offs between geographic vs topical vs popularity partitioning
Precise thresholds for politeness delays and concurrency per host under heavy scale
Optimal data structures for URL frontier and content seen for huge scale (Bloom filters vs hash sets) given false positive costs
Detailed prioritization scoring methodologies for URLs (PageRank, traffic, update frequency) and how to get/compute these scores at scale
Handling dynamic web content (JavaScript generated) and paginated or session-based URLs not covered
Cost model estimates for infrastructure at scale including bandwidth, storage, and running thousands of crawler workers
Failure modes and recovery semantics for transient network errors vs permanent host unavailability
Trade-offs in extracting and storing text only vs storing HTML plus text vs extracting metadata for better filtering

research_questions: What comprehensive strategies exist for seed URL selection to maximize coverage and refresh rate?
How to compute and update URL priority scores at scale efficiently?
What are best practices for crawl politeness delay tuning under heavy distributed load?
How to handle crawling modern dynamic websites with client-side rendering?
What is the cost breakdown for operating a PB-scale crawler cluster including storage/bandwidth?
Which data structures are best suited for URL and content deduplication at multi-billion scale?
How to implement fault tolerance to avoid duplicated crawling and data loss during node failures?
How to incorporate legal/privacy compliance into crawler design and operation?

research.research_summary: A technically credible crawler for LLM training should use a frontier that separates prioritization from politeness, because classic FIFO/BFS alone causes host bursts and ignores page importance. The strongest academic guidance is to score URLs using a combination of page quality/importance and historical change rate, then store those URLs in a frontier with front queues for priority and back queues for per-host politeness. For freshness, recrawl scheduling should be driven by observed change frequency and value/importance, rather than uniform revisits. At web scale, deduplication should use a fast approximate prefilter (e.g. Bloom filter) plus durable exact/near-duplicate handling; Nutch-style dedup groups same-content pages by digest and keeps a canonical representative. For modern sites, JavaScript rendering requires a secondary rendering path (for example a headless browser), but this should be used selectively because it is much more expensive than raw HTTP fetching. For fault tolerance, a queue with visibility timeout and dead-letter handling is a sound pattern: SQS documents that messages become visible again when not deleted before the visibility timeout, and repeated failures can be routed to a DLQ. For crawl politeness and compliance, RFC 9309 defines robots.txt as the protocol crawlers should honor, but Google’s documentation explicitly says fields such as crawl-delay are not supported by Googlebot; therefore, politeness delay should be enforced by the crawler itself, not assumed from robots.txt. For legal/privacy compliance, a production crawler should treat robots.txt as an access preference signal, not a security boundary, and also support publisher-specific crawler controls and content-policy signals where available. Official documentation from OpenAI and Google confirms robots.txt-based crawler controls are actively used in the ecosystem. The remaining major uncertainty is exact capacity/cost sizing for a PB-scale cluster, which depends heavily on fetch rate, average payload size, recrawl frequency, and whether dynamic rendering is enabled on a significant fraction of URLs.
